title: Family
author: Martin, Chris
summary: Chris Martin's personal essay identifies the hardest aspect of fatherhood not as sleep deprivation, lost personal time, or the unpredictability of toddlerhood, but as the constant effort to hold daughters as gifts rather than possessions. Writing from a Christian stewardship framework, Martin argues that the fundamental parenting error is the attempt to close one's hands around children, to protect them by becoming their god rather than their shepherd. The essay reflects on the tension between deep parental love and appropriate parental surrender: the recognition that children have a heavenly Father whose will takes precedence over their earthly father's instinct to control. Martin names the specific failure modes that arise when this tension is mismanaged, including over-protection, anxiety, and burden-bearing that does not belong to the parent. The essay's practical upshot is an open-handed posture toward children: stewarding them as gifts given in trust rather than securing them as possessions.
points: Martin's counterintuitive claim reframes the hardest part of fatherhood: not physical sacrifices or logistical demands, but the sustained effort to remain a steward rather than an owner of children entrusted to a father.

The stewardship model has a specific psychological implication in that it resists over-protection: a father who understands his daughters as given, not possessed, is less likely to bear on their behalf the anxiety that belongs elsewhere.

Closing your hands around gifts is Martin's phrase for the parenting error of over-investment in controlling outcomes, producing caginess, over-protection, and the substitution of a father's judgment for faith.

The open-handed posture toward children is counter-cultural: it requires parents to tolerate risk and uncertainty for their children rather than eliminating it, which runs against every parenting-culture instinct that equates good parenting with protection.

Martin situates fatherhood within a larger framework in which all of life's resources including time, talent, money, relationships, and suffering are gifts to be stewarded, not possessions to be controlled, and failing to remember this corrupts both the fathering and the father.
quotes: Being a dad is simultaneously the best and hardest role I've ever had to play in my life. I recognize that sort of sentiment may be cliche, but I do not care because it is true. I am grateful to be the dad of two little girls, ages six and two-and-a-half.

One of the more common parenting reflections I've heard from people over the years is that parenting is often the most difficult in the toddler and teenage years--before the age of three and after the age of 13. Having one child on either side of that three-year-old checkpoint, I understand the logic here and don't disagree that it gets a bit less difficult as kids get a bit more independent. But of course we parents would be mistaken to believe parenting somehow gets easy as independence blooms.

These struggles may be less of an assault on the senses than overnight wakings and overflowing diapers, but they are struggles nonetheless. Without a doubt, one of the most difficult parts of parenting for me on a most practical level has been the evaporation of personal time and space that comes with being a parent. I am a generally quiet and introverted person who likes my personal space and a quiet room for long reading sessions.

But sacrificing my personal preferences has not been the most difficult part of parenting. The hardest part of parenting, for me, is remembering that my beautiful daughters aren't really mine. Stewardship All the Way Down Best as I can tell, the Christian life is all about stewardship." Page 1 5. "What am I going to do with the money God has given me? What am I going to do with the career God has given me? What am I going to do with the home God has given me?

What am I going to do with the suffering God has given me? What am I going to do with the family God has given me? Everything I have, including my role as a father, has been generously given to me by my Father, the God of the universe--including my daughters.
